newsitem.title: USA: Clinton NATO choice meant to settle fierce debate.
newsitem.headline: Clinton NATO choice meant to settle fierce debate.

text.p: In rejecting European pressure to include Romania and Slovenia among new NATO members President Bill Clinton moved to settle a fierce debate that threatened to mar the accomplishment of NATO expansion.

With some European leaders, including German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, coming out this week in favour of Romania, Clinton finally showed his hand in insisting that only Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic should be admitted in the first wave.
NATO is a consensus organisation and "this is the three around which there is consensus" both in the alliance and in the U.S. government, one senior administration official told Reuters.

"This is a momentous event. The alliance is very important and we want to make sure as we move forward we maintain its basic strength, that we move in a steady and deliberate way, not biting off more than we can chew," the official said.
The best way to accomplish that is to "integrate some new members as we go along and not do it all at once," he added.

Until Thursday, when the White House announced Clinton's decision, Washington had been publicly coy about its position, although officials privately made it clear for some time that the government consensus did not favour Romania and Slovenia.
The main argument in favour of bringing Romania and Slovenia into NATO now is that their admittance would round out the alliance's vulnerable southern tier.

With a population of 22 million, Romania is much more important strategically than Slovenia, which has a population of 2 million. But its very size also makes Romania a relatively difficult country for NATO to digest.

For various reasons, U.S. officials believe that Romania -- which is strongly supported by Germany, France and several other European states -- and Slovenia -- backed by Italy -- need to work more on democratic, economic, political and military reforms before being accepted for NATO membership.

Romania elected a reformist government last November but U.S. officials say more time is needed to see if free market democracy really takes hold in the country, which was ruled by a communist dictatorship until 1989.
Also, U.S. officials say, leaving Romania and Slovenia out of the mix now more surely guarantees that NATO's move this year to take in new members will not be the last.
In part because they have support from other NATO members and have lobbied frantically to be admitted this year, both are seen as strong contenders for a second-round expansion.
It is a tenet of U.S. policy that NATO's door must remain open to new members from Europe into the indefinite future.

Cost is another concern. The latest U.S. study suggests the alliance will have to pay $35 billion over the next 12 years to expand with the U.S. share only $200 million annually. But many people suspect that figure is too low.

NATO leaders are to formally invite the former Warsaw Pact states to join the alliance at a July 8-9 summit in Madrid. The Republican-dominated U.S. Senate, like legislatures in NATO's 15 other members countries, must ratify the expansion.

The U.S. announcement also followed a meeting in Strasbourg, France on Tuesday at which European centrist leaders including Kohl called for Romania to be included in the first wave of new NATO members.
The group, which includes the leaders of NATO members Germany, Spain, Italy, Luxembourg and Belgium, pledged to try to overcome U.S. reluctance to invite Romania in.
Despite this, U.S. officials believe it is likely that at Madrid, Kohl will ultimately side with Clinton.
The United States is NATO's dominant member and, with Germany, pays more than 50 percent of alliance costs.

One sign of the sensitivity of the decision on new members was that Clinton did not announce the U.S. position himself. One source familiar with the U.S. position said Washington did not want to be seen as throwing its weight about.

"(Defense Secretary William) Cohen is in Brussels now to inform (NATO Secretary-General) Javier Solana of the U.S. position. Solana is charged with building a consensus and the final action will be taken in Madrid," the source said.
"Deference is being shown to the NATO process. This is our view, but there are 16 members" of NATO, the source said.
Asked if the United States might be overruled on the matter by other NATO members, White House press secretary Mike McCurry told reporters: "That is not likely."
